DILG BAGONG PILIPINAS Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA cor. Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City euv.pll ATTY. CHRISTIAN LLOYD S. SANTOS clsantos@santos-law.com Dear Atty. Santos: This has reference to your Letter dated February 26, 2025, requesting this Department's opinion on whether a municipal administrator, who is a lawyer, may engage in the private practice of law, specifically by acting as a defense counsel in criminal cases and defendants' counsel in a civil case. Hence, you have raised the following issues: I. 2. 3. Is a municipal administrator, being a full-time government official, allowed to engage in private law practice, particularly as a defense lawyer for an accused in a criminal case in Regional Trial Court (RTC) and defendants' lawyer in a civil case? Would such an engagement violate existing laws, ethical rules, or jurisprudence, including the Local Government Code (LGC) and the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA)? If such practice is prohibited, what are the legal consequences for a municipal administrator who engages in private law practice while in office? With regard to the first and second issues, we deem it prudent to discuss the same in one discussion. As a general rule, public officials and employees are prohibited from engaging in the private practice of profession.l This is pursuant to the time-honored principle that public office is a public trust and that public officials and employees must uphold public interest over personal interest.2 However, Section 7(b)(2) of Republic Act (R.A.) No. 6713, or the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees states the conditions in allowing limited practice of profession, to wit: "Section 7. Prohibited Acts and Transactions. — In addition to acts Section 7(b)(2), R.A. No. 6713 or the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees: Engage in the private practice of their profession unless authorized by the Constitution or law, provided, that such practice will not conflict or tend to conflict with their official functions. 2 Section 2, R.A. No. 6713. "Matino, Mahusay at Maaasahan" Trunkline NO. (02) 8876 3454

and omissions of public officials and employees now prescribed in the Constitution and existing laws, the following shall constitute prohibited acts and transactions of any public official and employee and are hereby declared to be unlawful: xxx (b) Outside employment and other activities related thereto. officials and employees during their incumbency shall not: xxx - Public (2) Engage in the private practice of their profession unless authorized by the Constitution or law, provided, that such practice will not conflict or tend to conflict with their official functions." The municipal administrator, as a local appointive official, is subject to the prohibition on private practice of profession in accordance with the provisions under R.A. No. 6713 and other pertinent laws and regulations. Nevertheless, as authorized under the aforementioned provision, he/she, as a lawyer, may be allowed limited practice of profession, provided that it will not be in conflict with his/her official functions as a municipal administrator. Furthermore, Section 136 of the 2017 Omnibus Rules on Appointments and Other Human Resource Actions3 imposes the following requirements in order to grant such exemption: "Sec. 136. No officer or employee, whether in a permanent or regular, capacity, temporary, casual, or hold-over, shall engage directly or indirectly in any private business or practice of profession. Exemptions may be allowed, subject to the limitations provided under RA No. 6713 and other special laws. Provided, further that the following requirements/conditions are met: a. Written permission from head of agency must be secured and renewed annually; b. Time devoted outside of office hours shall not impair in any way the efficiency of the officer or employee nor pose a conflict or tend to conflict with the official functions and must be fixed by the head of agency; and c. Government facilities, equipment and supplies shall not be used while engaged in private business or practice of profession As such, it is mandatory for the municipal administrator to comply with the above- mentioned conditions in order to validly engage in the private practice of profession. With Civil Service Commission Memorandum Circular No. 24, s. 2017. Page 2 of 4

regard to the first requirement, the municipal administrator should request the authority from the Secretary of the Interior and Local Government (SILG), being the head of the Department, pursuant to the case of Monares v. Munozd. In said case, the Supreme Court also cited Section 12, Rule XVIII of the Revised Civil Service Rules which provides: "Sec. 12. No officer or employee shall engage directly in any private business, vocation, or profession or be connected with any commercial, credit, agricultural, or industrial undertaking without a written permission from the head of Department: Provided, That this prohibition will be absolute in the case of those officers and employees whose duties and responsibilities require that their entire time be at the disposal of the Government: Provided, further, That if an employee is granted permission to engage in outside activities, the time so devoted outside of office hours should be fixed by the chief of the agency to the end that it will not impair in any way the efficiency of the officer or employee." x x x Based on the foregoing provisions, if there is an authority granted by the SILG, the municipal administrator may engage in the practice of law subject to other conditions, such as ensuring that no official working hours will be used for his/her private practice. Stated differently, the municipal administrator is prohibited from using government time for his/her practice of profession. Moreover, it is important to note that the duties and responsibilities of the municipal administrator should not be prejudiced nor compromised by his/her private practice of profession. He/She should make sure that there will be no conflict of interest between the performance of duty as a public servant and the duty as counsel when representing clients in litigation. Further, may we invite your attention to Section 21, Canon III of the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability.5 "SECTION 21. Lawyers in government service; conflict of interest. - A lawyer currently serving in the government shall not practice law privately, unless otherwise authorized by the Constitution, the law or applicable Civil Service rules and regulations. If allowed, private practice shall be upon the express authority of the lawyer's superior, for a stated specified purpose or engagement, and only during an approved leave of absence. However, the lawyer shall not represent an interest adverse to the government." All things considered, if the municipal administrator has engaged in private legal practice without complying first with the conditions for limited practice, specifically without securing any written authority from the SILG, such practice shall be considered prohibited. Thus, for the third issue, the municipal administrator may be held administratively, civilly, or criminally liable for engaging in prohibited practice. Under Section II of R.A. No. 6713, 4 A.c. No. 5582, January 24, 2017. A.M No. 22-09-01-SC Page 3 of 4

committing any violation of its provisions by a public official or employee may lead to administrative penalties such as suspension, imposition of a fine, or removal from office, depending on the gravity of the offense. In case there is another law that provides for a heavier penalty, such as imprisonment, he/she shall be prosecuted under said law. In addition, the municipal administrator, being a lawyer, may be held administratively liable by the Supreme Coun for engaging in prohibited private practice. He/She may be reprimanded, suspended from the practice of law, or disbarred, especially if there is a conflict of interest. In Abella v. Cruzabra6, the respondent, who was a Deputy Register of Deeds, was found guilty of engaging in notarial practice without written authority from the Secretary of Justice and was reprimanded by the Supreme Court. In the case of Yumol, Jr. v. Ferrer, Sry, the lawyer who was employed in the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) was suspended for failure to obtain written authority and approval from the CHR before engaging in private practice. Please note that this opinion is based solely on the facts disclosed in the letter and the issues raised therein. This opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of the courts and competent authorities. We hope to have addressed your concern accordingly. Very truly yours, BY AUTHORITY OF THE SECRETARY: ATTY. ROMEO P. BENITEZ Undersecretary for External, Legal and Legislative Affairs OUSELLARPB/LLLS-LRALLO/nab 6 A.c. No. 5688, June 4, 2009 ' A.c.
